newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish ex-communists vow 25 pct economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Polish ex-communists vow 25 pct economic growth.

text.p: Poland's ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), launching its campaign for September elections, promised 25 percent economic growth over four years and a radical drop in inflation if elected.

The party, which held an electoral convention on Sunday, said it would strive to boost industrial output by 40 percent, curb inflation to about six percent from 14.6 percent in May and lower unemployment if it won the Septembr 21 polls.

"The SLD promises...a continued growth and solving social problems. Our electoral slogan is 'Good today, better tomorrow,"' ex-communist Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told a news conference after the convention.

Cimoszewicz, whose group is in power since 1993 along with the Peasant Party, claimed credit for the country's economic success and vowed to pursue financial stability policies and continue efforts to bring Poland into the European Union and NATO.
"I am convinced that just as we have brought Poland to the threshold of the European Union, we will be able to bring it to full membership," he said.
The SLD pledged to achieve its economic goals by attracting more foreign investors, through more investment reliefs, reduced taxes and improved telecommunications and transport links.
The party pledged to continue privatisation with the aim of boosting the private sector's contribution to gross domestic product from its current 60 percent to 75-80 percent within four years.
Cimoszewicz said his party's other priorities were education, public security and upgrading the armed forces to NATO standards.

The SLD's programme said that unlike its main electoral rival, the opposition rightist Solidarity Election Action (AWS), the SLD would continue to advocate a secular state and the right of women to have abortions.
The former communists are running neck-and-neck with the AWS, a group of rightist parties clustered around the Solidarity trade union.
With both groups each credited with more than 20 percent support, analysts say smaller parties are likely to hold the balance of power in the next parliament.
Cimoszewicz confirmed that in the event of a hung poll the ex-communists would consider other coalition partners other than their present allies, the Peasants.
SLD officials have made clear the party would also consider a coaliton with the centrist Union for Freeedom and leftist Labour Union. 291528 GMT jun 97
